title: “Wrong number” turns into a crypto tip
setup: A stranger texted you by mistake two weeks ago. You've been chatting casually since. Today:

messages.text: Sorry, is this Kevin? We're still on for golf Sunday? ⛳️
So glad I texted you by mistake 😊 My uncle trades crypto and I made $38,000 last month on his platform. I can show you how. Start with just $500!

options.label: Try $500 — she showed you screenshots of her gains
options.feedback: The fake platform showed big “profits” until you invested more. Then it demanded “taxes” to withdraw. You got nothing back.

options.label: Stop replying and block the number
options.feedback: “Wrong number” texts that turn friendly and then pitch investing are a known pattern for crypto investment scams.

options.label: Invest a small amount and withdraw it to test the platform
options.feedback: Scammers often let you withdraw a little to build trust, then take much more.

redFlags: A friendship that started with a “wrong number”
Lavish profits and a special platform
safestAction: Don't invest with anyone you've only met online. Block, report, and never download a trading app someone sends you.

followUps.setup: Three weeks later your dashboard shows $12,400. You ask to withdraw it.

messages.text: I'd like to take out $12,400 please
So happy for you!! 🎉 The platform holds 15% capital gains tax before release — $1,860. My uncle says pay it and the whole balance lands same day.

options.label: Pay the $1,860 — you'll net over $10,000
options.feedback: The $12,400 was never real. No exchange collects tax before releasing your own money; the “tax” is the last squeeze.

options.label: Refuse, stop paying anything, and report it
options.feedback: Right. Money already sent is likely gone, but the fee would have been gone too. Report it to IC3.

options.label: Ask Amy to cover the fee from her own account
options.feedback: There is no Amy. You'll get sympathy, a story about her funds being locked, and the same demand.

title: Investment group promising guaranteed returns
setup: Someone adds you to a group chat called “Wealth Builders VIP.”

content.body: Welcome! Our AI trading signals deliver GUARANTEED 30% monthly returns with zero risk. Members made $2.1M last week 📈💰 Only 20 new VIP seats left. Message me to join today.

options.label: Message him to grab a VIP seat
options.feedback: The “VIP fee” and your first deposit disappeared into a fake trading account.

options.label: Leave the group and report it
options.feedback: No legitimate investment guarantees high returns with no risk. Leaving is exactly right.

options.label: Watch for a few weeks to see if it's real
options.feedback: No money lost, but these groups are full of fake members posting fake wins to reel you in.

redFlags: Added to a group you never joined
safestAction: Ignore unsolicited investment pitches. Check any adviser at investor.gov before investing a dollar.

title: “Convert your savings to gold — a courier will collect it”
setup: A caller says he's a federal agent investigating identity theft involving your accounts.

messages.text: Your identity was used in a money laundering case. Your bank accounts will be frozen.
To protect your assets, withdraw your savings and buy gold. A secure government courier will pick it up for safekeeping. Tell no one — it's a sealed investigation.

options.label: Buy the gold and hand it to the courier
options.feedback: The “courier” worked for the scammers. The gold was gone the moment you handed it over.

options.label: Hang up and tell someone you trust
options.feedback: No government agency will ever ask you to hand cash or gold to a courier. Talking to someone breaks the scammer's spell of secrecy.

options.label: Ask for the agent's badge number and verify it
options.feedback: They'll supply convincing fake credentials. Nothing they give you can make this request real.

redFlags: Told to buy gold or withdraw cash
safestAction: Hang up. Government agencies never tell you to move money, buy gold, or hand anything to a courier.

title: Told to deposit cash in a Bitcoin ATM
setup: A caller says he's from your bank's security department. He keeps you on the line while you drive.

messages.text: Good, you've withdrawn the cash. Now go into the gas station on the corner. There's a Bitcoin machine by the door.
I'll text you a QR code. Scan it at the machine and insert the cash. That moves it into your secure wallet.

options.label: Insert the cash and scan the QR code
options.feedback: The QR code was the scammer's wallet. Crypto ATM deposits are nearly impossible to recover.

options.label: Hang up and walk into your bank branch
options.feedback: No bank or government agency will ever send you to a Bitcoin ATM. Hanging up is always the answer.

options.label: Ask the store clerk to hold the phone while you think
options.feedback: You didn't pay yet, but you're still under their control. Ending the call is what breaks it.

redFlags: Any instruction to use a Bitcoin ATM
Kept on the phone the whole time
QR code texted by the caller
safestAction: Anyone who tells you to pay with cryptocurrency or a Bitcoin ATM is a scammer. Hang up.

title: Quarterly retirement statement
setup: You have a retirement account through work. Early in the month, this arrives.

content.subject: Your Q3 statement is ready
content.body: Hi Sam, your quarterly statement for your employer retirement plan is now available. For your security, this email contains no personal account details. Sign in to your account to view it.
content.footer: Keystone Retirement will never ask for your password or Social Security number by email.

options.label: Open the Keystone app or your saved bookmark to view it
options.feedback: Expected timing, no request for info, and you went in through your own app. Perfect habit.

options.label: Report it as phishing
options.feedback: No harm, but this one was real. Signing in through your app would have confirmed it.

options.label: Reply with your SSN to get the statement faster
options.feedback: Even with a real company, email isn't safe for your SSN. It was exposed and misused.

redFlags: Routine timing — quarterly statements are expected
Contains no links or requests for info
Reminds you they won't ask for passwords
safestAction: For financial accounts, sign in through the app or a bookmark you saved — never through links, even in real emails.

title: Video ad of a famous investor endorsing a trading app
setup: A video ad shows a well-known billionaire investor, voice and all, recommending an app.

content.body: 🎥 “I've never shared this publicly. This AI trading app turned $250 into $9,400 for everyday Americans in 30 days. Banks hate it.”
content.subject: EXCLUSIVE: Billionaire reveals his secret AI app

options.label: Sign up and deposit the $250 minimum
options.feedback: The video was AI-generated. A “broker” then called and pressured you into larger deposits you couldn't withdraw.

options.label: Scroll past and report the ad
options.feedback: Celebrity endorsements in ads can be faked with AI. Real opportunities don't come from urgent social media ads.

options.label: Give them your phone number for more info
options.feedback: No money lost yet, but you'll get relentless high-pressure calls from fake brokers.

redFlags: Celebrity faces and voices can be deepfaked
Unbelievable returns in a short time
Fake news site and midnight deadline
safestAction: Treat investment ads on social media as scams by default. Research any platform independently and check it at investor.gov.
